passage:
I'm Parveen, and I sat next to Jasleen in the project lab for those two weeks. On the first Monday Jasleen said, "Three days, if nothing goes wrong," and started the report straight away.
By Wednesday the printer had jammed, the group chat was buzzing, and nobody could tell what the second step meant. On Friday the laptop would not turn on. Jasleen borrowed mine for a night. Then a teacher changed the format.
It ended up taking ten days. Jasleen looked tired and kept saying, "It should have been simple." I can't say what Jasleen was thinking, but the three-day number was never mentioned again.

qa.q: How many days did the report finally take?
What did Jasleen seem to feel at the end of the two weeks?
qa.a: Jasleen looked tired and kept saying it should have been simple, which suggests frustration, though Parveen cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do the next time a project needs an estimate?
qa.a: Jasleen could think of what usually goes wrong, such as breakdowns and unclear steps, and add time for it, since the best case rarely happens.

qa.q: How does Parveen see the ten days?
qa.a: Parveen watched from the next seat, lent a laptop, and cannot know Jasleen's thoughts, but saw that the three-day plan was never mentioned again.

grounding: A student estimates a project from the best case, and interruptions, a broken laptop and unclear steps stretch it to ten days.

passage:
Monday: Rukmini sketched her plan for the app project. "Design on Monday, code on Tuesday, test Wednesday. Three days, done." Her friend Jagdish asked, "What if something goes wrong?" "It won't. I know this stuff."

Thursday: She was still stuck on the login screen; the tutorial steps didn't match the new version. Her laptop fan started making a grinding sound. On Friday it wouldn't turn on at all. The repair shop said four days.

The following Wednesday: Working on a borrowed laptop, between classes and a cousin's engagement, Rukmini finally finished testing. Ten days, not three. She looked at her Monday plan and laughed weakly. "I planned for everything going right. Nothing did."

qa.q: How long did the repair shop say the laptop would take?
How did Rukmini feel when she looked at her Monday plan?
qa.a: She felt tired and a bit foolish, laughing weakly at a plan that assumed everything would go right.

qa.q: What would you change first about Rukmini's estimate?
qa.a: Plan for the likely case, not the best one: leave extra days for unclear steps, breakdowns and life events.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see how it turned out?
qa.a: Jagdish, who asked what could go wrong, may feel sympathetic but not surprised.

grounding: A student estimates a project from the best case at three days, and it takes ten with interruptions, a broken laptop and unclear steps.

subtype: Approach: estimates from the best case and expects to finish early [Pitfall]
passage: Sonali, you asked why I always add days to every plan. Let me tell your Bhavna Masi's secret. When I was twenty, in my final year, I had a model to build for my architecture thesis. I told my professor, "Three days. Two for cutting, one for assembling." I said it proudly. Day one, the cutter blade broke and the shop was closed. Day two, my roommate had a fever and I took her to the clinic. Day four, I found the drawing had an error, and I had to redo the roof. Then the power went out for a whole evening. It took me ten days. My professor wasn't angry, just said, "You planned for a perfect week. Nobody gets one." I've never forgotten it.

qa.q: How many days did young Bhavna say the model would take?
qa.a: Three days: two for cutting, one for assembling.

qa.q: How did young Bhavna feel when she gave her estimate?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident, sure everything would go smoothly.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Bhavna have planned better?
qa.a: When she gave the estimate; allowing for things going wrong, like broken tools or errors, would have made it realistic.

qa.q: How might the roommate have felt being taken to the clinic?
qa.a: The roommate probably felt grateful for the help, though it cost Bhavna a day.

grounding: An elder recalls estimating a project from the best case at three days, and it taking ten with interruptions and problems.
